extracted.intended_audience: students of classical geometry / advanced high-school or undergraduate readers studying geometric constructions and constructibility
extracted.subtask_description: Exposition of classical results and methods for geometric constructions: constructibility (algebraic/transcendental distinctions), inversion in a circle, compass-only (Mascheroni) constructions, mechanical curves and linkages, and applications (Apollonius, pentagon, etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Constructible numbers characterization
rubrics_metrics.description: A segment (number) is constructible iff the number lies in a field F* that can be reached by the successive adjunction of square roots to the rational field F0.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hence all members of any such field are algebraic numbers (satisfy algebraic equations with integer coefficients); constructibility reduces to algebraic (in particular quadratic-extension) criteria. Used to reduce geometric constructibility questions (e.g., regular heptagon, squaring the circle) to algebraic/transcendence properties of specific numbers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of Rational Root Theorem to test constructibility/rationality
rubrics_metrics.description: To show a candidate number y is not rational, test rational roots of its minimal polynomial; if the only possible rational roots (from integer divisors) do not satisfy the polynomial, the number is irrational.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: For y satisfying y^3 + y^2 - 2y -1 = 0, assuming a rational root r/s (coprime) leads to divisibility constraints showing only possible values ±1, which fail — thus no rational roots. This argument supports non-constructibility when combined with the constructible-number characterization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transcendence obstructs classical constructions (squaring the circle)
rubrics_metrics.description: If a required length equals a transcendental number (e.g., π or √π), it cannot belong to any field obtained by successive square-root adjunctions (all such fields consist of algebraic numbers), so the corresponding straightedge-and-compass construction is impossible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historical route: Hermite proved e transcendental; Lindemann extended method to prove π transcendental, settling impossibility of squaring the circle by classical constructions. The text notes proof requires advanced analysis beyond scope.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of inversion in a circle
rubrics_metrics.description: Given a circle C with center O and radius r, the image P' of a point P under inversion is the point on ray OP (same side of O) such that OP · OP' = r^2.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consequences: P and P' are inverse points; inversion interchanges inside/outside of C; points on C are fixed; O itself has no finite image (corresponds to point at infinity). Inversion sets up a bijection between points of the plane and their images (interpreting O ↔ infinity).

rubrics_metrics.name: Images of lines and circles under inversion (four cases)
rubrics_metrics.description: Under inversion: (a) a line through O becomes a line through O; (b) a line not through O becomes a circle through O; (c) a circle through O becomes a line not through O; (d) a circle not through O becomes a circle not through O.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proofs use similarity and circle properties (e.g., perpendicular from O to a line, constant ratios leading to fixed diameters); these cases are fundamental for transforming geometric problems via inversion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inversion preserves angle magnitudes (conformal) and reverses orientation
rubrics_metrics.description: The angle between two curves (angle between tangents) is invariant in magnitude under inversion: the image curves meet at the same angle; however inversion reverses the sense (orientation) of the angle.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: By continuity of secants tending to tangents and triangle similarity arguments one shows angle preservation; immediate corollaries: orthogonality and tangency of circles/lines are preserved under inversion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Geometric construction of inverse points (compass-only procedure)
rubrics_metrics.description: A point P' inverse to a given point P with respect to circle C (center O, radius r) can be constructed using compass-only methods: for P exterior to C use intersections of circles to locate P'; if P is interior, reduce to the exterior case by finding a multiple R on OP outside C and scaling back.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Procedure details: with center P and radius OP draw arc meeting C at R,S; with centers R,S draw arcs radius r to meet at O and P_r on OP; similarity of triangles gives OP·OP' = r^2. For interior P, find R on OP with OR = n·OP outside C, construct R', then deduce P' from OR' and scaling. This construction underpins many compass-only constructions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mascheroni theorem (compass alone suffices)
rubrics_metrics.description: All geometric constructions possible with straightedge and compass can be performed with the compass alone (interpreting a line as given by any two points on it).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mascheroni's result relies on constructing, with compass only, the four fundamental operations: (1) draw a circle with given center and radius; (2) find intersections of two circles; (3) find intersections of a straight line and a circle; (4) find intersections of two straight lines. The text shows how inversion and compass constructions yield (3) and (4). Examples provided: doubling a segment, bisecting segments/arcs, constructing the center of a circle given only its circumference.

rubrics_metrics.name: Four fundamental compass constructions (basis for Mascheroni)
rubrics_metrics.description: Every standard ruler-and-compass construction reduces to repetitions of these four elementary constructions: (1) drawing a circle with given center and radius; (2) finding intersections of two circles; (3) finding intersections of a straight line and a circle; (4) finding intersections of two straight lines.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: First two are immediate with compass; the latter two are achieved via inversion-based constructions and compass-only constructions of inverse points. Proving these four are possible suffices to prove Mascheroni's theorem.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compass-only construction for intersection of a circle and a line
rubrics_metrics.description: Given circle C and line through two points A,B, construct points of intersection X,X' by: draw circles with centers A and B and radii AO and BO meeting at P; find Q inverse to P w.r.t. C; draw circle center Q radius QO; its intersections with C are the required points.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reason: circle through X,X',0 is inverse of line AB; points on circumference are self-inverse; uses earlier compass-only inverse-point construction. Special cases (line through center) treated separately by midpoint/arc methods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compass-only construction for intersection of two lines
rubrics_metrics.description: Given two lines AB and A'B', pick an arbitrary circle C, construct the circles that are inverses of the two lines (with respect to C); these circles intersect at O and Y; the inverse X of Y is the intersection point of the original lines.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Method reduces finding line intersections to circle intersections and inverse-point constructions, all achievable with compass-only tools following the Mascheroni framework.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examples of compass-only constructions (midpoint, bisecting arcs, center of circle)
rubrics_metrics.description: Specific compass constructions given: bisect a segment AB by marking off three arcs of radius AB and then using inversion; bisect an arc AB of circle with center O via sequence of arc constructions; find center of circle given only circumference by constructing an inverse point.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Detailed step-by-step constructions are included in the text (with diagrams); proofs rely on properties of inverses and congruent/isoceles/ equilateral triangle constructions. These illustrate practical applications of the general Mascheroni result.

rubrics_metrics.name: Steiner straightedge result and its necessary condition
rubrics_metrics.description: The straightedge alone can perform all ruler-and-compass constructions provided a single fixed circle together with its center is given; the given circle and its center cannot be dispensed with.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reason: if only a circle but not its center is given, there exists a plane transformation fixing the circle and carrying lines to lines but moving the center, showing impossibility of constructing the center with straightedge alone. Steiner's constructions use projective methods; details deferred.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mechanical curves allow solving higher-degree algebraic equations
rubrics_metrics.description: If instruments exist to draw specified mechanical curves (e.g., hyperbola xy=k and parabola y=ax^2+bx+c), then intersections of these curves produce solutions of algebraic equations such as cubics: ax^3+bx^2+cx=k.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: By parametrizing with y from the hyperbola and parabola and eliminating y, the x-coordinates of intersections are the roots of the cubic. Thus allowing certain non-circular instruments enlarges constructible set beyond classical compass-and-straightedge limitations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cycloid/hypocycloid/epicycloid closure condition
rubrics_metrics.description: When a circle of radius r rolls on/inside/outside another circle of radius R, the resulting (hypo/epi)cycloid closes up after n circuits and consists of m arches precisely when R/r = m/n is a rational ratio; special cases (e.g., R=2r) yield simple loci.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If R/r is an integer the point returns after one circuit; if R/r = m/n in lowest terms, the curve closes after n circuits and has m arches. Variations include point inside circle or on extension of radius producing different cycloid shapes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Linkage constructions realize algebraic curves via inversion (Peaucellier & Hart)
rubrics_metrics.description: Specific linkages (Peaucellier's 7-bar, Hart's 5-bar inversor) convert circular motion into exact rectilinear motion by enforcing a constant product OP·OQ (i.e., inversion relation), so a point Q traces a straight line as P traces a circle through O.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Details: Peaucellier's linkage imposes OP·OQ = t^2 - s^2 = r^2 constant, making P and Q inverse with respect to a circle of radius r; since inverse of a circle through O is a straight line, Q moves linearly. Hart's inversor uses equalities of rod lengths and ratios to obtain analogous constant OP·OQ. Other linkages can generate ellipses, hyperbolas, or any algebraic curve in principle.

rubrics_metrics.name: Behavior of families of circles under inversion
rubrics_metrics.description: A family of all circles passing through the inversion center O and another fixed point A is mapped to a family of straight lines radiating from A' (image of A); circles orthogonal to that family go to circles orthogonal to those lines. Circles tangent at O map to parallel lines.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These correspondences show how complex circle configurations transform into simpler line systems, enabling problem simplifications (visualized in diagrams). Orthogonality and tangency relations are preserved under inversion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inversion-based solution strategy for Apollonius' problem
rubrics_metrics.description: To construct a circle tangent externally to three given circles, increase radii by same d to arrange two given circles tangent at K, invert about K to transform two circles to parallel lines and the third to another circle; construct the circle tangent to these (easy), then invert back to obtain the Apollonius solution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Key observations: uniform radius increase corresponds to radial shift in solution (p→p−d); inversion simplifies the configuration to lines and one circle whose tangency relations are easier (radius r equals half distance between parallels); final inversion yields the desired circle. This exemplifies choosing an advantageous inversion center to reduce complexity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Repeated inversion/reflection phenomena (image families)
rubrics_metrics.description: Repeated reflection/inversion in multiple mirrors/circles produces infinite families of images (e.g., concentric circles between concentric circular mirrors) with sequences tending to infinity or concentrating about centers; configurations depend on relative positions of circles/mirrors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These phenomena explain visual effects of multiple reflections and have geometric descriptions via inversion sequences; special mirror constellations (equilateral triangle, rectangular isosceles) produce regular non-overlapping coverings.
